Lai Study 1 replication with VH estimators

Technical review of historical comparability, reporting scale, and slope-SD diagnostics

Technical summary

The replication succeeds on its primary like-for-like point-estimate check. On Lai’s historical reporting scale, our dual-BLUP analogue has negative bias near \(-.02\) for every random-effect correlation, closely matching Lai’s original dual-EB series. The previously suspected sign disagreement came from comparing that dual method with Lai’s separate slope-only EB series, whose bias changes sign with the random-effect correlation. Our 2S-PA and MSEM analogues also remain close to zero, as in the original results.

That conclusion is scale-specific. On the raw and common latent-slope-SD views, the dual-BLUP estimator is centrally near zero (with rare, very large failures), so much of its historical negative bias is attributable to Lai’s method-specific EB-slope-SD multiplier. In contrast, closed-form OLS remains negatively biased on the common scale, while Fuller, Fuller alpha-stepdown, 2S-PA, and MSEM are generally much closer to zero.

The interval results from the seven-method run are encouraging but not exact replications: our 2S-PA is somewhat conservative and our VH/Mplus MSEM somewhat anti-conservative relative to Lai’s original summaries, especially at \(J=30\). A historical-only eighth method now reproduces Lai’s original OpenMx MSEM and obtains the standardized estimate and delta-method SE directly from mxSE(stdbeta). It is added to the historical panels when its separate array has been completed and aggregated; it never enters the seven-method VH panels. Lai’s 2S-PAB and slope-only EB variants remain outside this refresh.

The production aggregate contains 486 DGM conditions, 7 methods, and 2,430,000 simulated data sets per raw reporting view. Its source is /proj/mnhallqlab/projects/blup_unshrinking/outputs/lai_study1_vh_production_20260731/lai_study1_vh_summary.csv.

Result at a glance

For the historical comparison at \(\beta_{Zu1}=.4\), the naïve dual-BLUP median trimmed bias is negative at every random-effect correlation (rho = -0.5: -0.022; rho = 0: -0.023; rho = 0.5: -0.021). This closely reproduces Lai’s original dual-EB \((u_0+u_1)\) series. The correlation-signed pattern in the original paper belongs to the two slope-only EB specifications, which are not in the seven-method VH bundle. 2S-PA remains near zero (rho = -0.5: 0.000; rho = 0: -0.000; rho = 0.5: -0.000) and the VH/Mplus MSEM is small and positive (rho = -0.5: 0.002; rho = 0: 0.001; rho = 0.5: 0.000) on this historical view. The source-faithful OpenMx MSEM add-on is complete and included in the historical panels. Its correlation-specific medians are rho = -0.5: 0.000; rho = 0: -0.000; rho = 0.5: -0.000.

On the common latent-SD VH view, the naïve dual-BLUP median is not itself the main issue; its distribution has 11 conditions with \(|\mathrm{mean\ bias}| > 1\), including a maximum of 5930.0. The report therefore shows its central behavior and its rare instability in separate panels rather than letting those failures flatten every other method’s plot.

Methods and terminology

The target is the effect of the level-2 covariate \(Z\) on the random slope \(u_1\). “Dual” means that the stage-2 regression uses both the random intercept \(u_0\) and random slope \(u_1\) as predictors; this is important when those random effects are correlated.

Estimator terminology used throughout this report
Method Stage-2 predictor or model Interpretive role
Oracle dual True simulated u0 and u1 Simulation benchmark; not available in applications
Naive dual BLUP Empirical-Bayes (BLUP) u0 and u1, treated as observed Shows attenuation/instability from ignoring first-stage uncertainty
Closed-form dual Closed-form corrected u0 and u1, treated as observed Separates corrected-score construction from stage-2 EIV correction
Fuller closed-form Closed-form corrected scores with their measurement-error covariance EIV-style correction using estimated first-stage error covariance
Fuller alpha-stepdown Fuller correction with alpha stepdown for a guarded correction Stabilized Fuller variant in the VH Study 2 bundle
2S-PA Lai two-stage path-analysis model fitted in OpenMx Direct Lai-method overlap for historical comparison
MSEM (VH/Mplus) Joint multilevel structural-equation model fitted in Mplus VH Study 2 latent-variable benchmark; historical comparison diagnostic
MSEM (original OpenMx; historical only) Lai’s original cross-level OpenMx MSEM; direct standardized algebra and mxSE delta-method SE Source-faithful historical benchmark; excluded from VH-primary seven-method comparisons

The first three methods use a two-predictor observed-score regression in stage 2. The distinction is whether those predictors are true random effects, shrunken EB estimates, or closed-form corrected scores. The Fuller methods also propagate the estimated measurement-error covariance into the stage-2 correction. 2S-PA and both MSEM implementations instead fit their own latent-variable/path models. The VH/Mplus MSEM is one of the seven primary methods. The original OpenMx MSEM is an eighth, historical-only diagnostic: its standardized effect and SE jointly account for uncertainty in the fitted latent slope SD through OpenMx’s delta method.

2. Historical Figure 2 analogue: compare like with like

This panel is the primary visual comparison with Lai’s Figure 2. It contains the three methods already available from the VH run (naive dual BLUP, 2S-PA, and VH/Mplus MSEM) plus Lai’s original OpenMx MSEM when the additive historical run is complete. It uses Lai’s method-specific historical standardization, Lai’s status_code == 0 retention rule, and a 20%-trimmed Monte Carlo bias. Lai’s published Figure 2 code plots six methods: 2S-PA, 2S-PAB, MSEM, EB \((u_0+u_1)\), centered EB, and uncentered EB. This analogue retains only the directly corresponding 2S-PA and dual-EB series, the current VH/Mplus MSEM diagnostic, and—when available—a source-faithful rerun of the original OpenMx MSEM. The table resolves the central replication question. Our dual-BLUP medians are about \(-.022\) across the three values of \(\rho\), versus roughly \(-.024\) to \(-.026\) for Lai’s dual-EB method. Both 2S-PA implementations are essentially unbiased; the VH/Mplus MSEM differs slightly in sign but remains small. The original OpenMx MSEM row, when present, is the decisive like-for-like implementation check because it uses Lai’s original model and delta-method interval rather than reconstructing a standardized interval from a raw Mplus path. The slope-only centered and uncentered EB lines in Lai’s figure do change sign with \(\rho\), but they answer a different stage-2 regression question and are not represented here. The current Figure 2 analogue is therefore a strong replication for the overlapping point estimators, not evidence of a contradiction.

Historical coverage and Type I error analogues

The next two panels mimic Lai’s Figures 3 and 4 using the same historical methods, historical scale, and status_code == 0 retention rule. Coverage is the proportion of retained 95% intervals containing the truth. The Type I panel is limited to \(\beta_{Zu1}=0\) and uses two-sided 95% CI exclusion as the rejection rule for the three methods reconstructed from the VH output. The original OpenMx MSEM add-on instead stores and uses Lai’s exact normal-Wald p < .05 definition. These rules ordinarily agree, but keeping the provenance explicit prevents the reconstructed VH/Mplus interval from being mistaken for Lai’s delta-method interval.

The reference lines are .95 for coverage and .05 for Type I error. The table uses condition-level rates (not a pooled replication denominator), so it describes how performance varies across the Lai design. Interpret a departure from either reference together with the matching bias panel and the number of retained replications: a nominal interval result can change when the historical reporting multiplier or status-code retention changes.

For these three overlapping methods, 2S-PA is slightly conservative overall: mean coverage is 95.9% and mean CI-based Type I error is 4.0%. Naïve dual BLUP averages 93.3% coverage and 5.6% Type I error; MSEM averages 94.3% and 5.6%, respectively. The strongest MSEM departure is in the \(J=30\) cells, where its mean coverage is 91.8% and its mean Type I error is 8.1%. The source-faithful OpenMx MSEM averages 95.9% coverage and 4.0% Type I error overall; at J = 30 the corresponding values are 96.0% and 4.0%. Relative to Lai’s original summaries, current dual-BLUP coverage and Type I error are close. Current 2S-PA is more conservative (about 96% coverage and 4% Type I error versus about 95% and 4.5% originally), while MSEM is more anti-conservative (about 94% and 5.7% versus about 96% and 4.2%). The historical OpenMx row now separates a model/software/interval-construction difference from a DGM difference. Those are practical inference differences worth tracing; they do not overturn the point-estimate replication.

Paired Mplus–OpenMx audit: two mechanisms, not one

The completed paired-engine audit regenerates the exact data for two close and two maximally divergent seed/condition pairs, then retains all Mplus input and output files. It compares the current Mplus specification (whose retained output identifies its default estimator as MLR), an explicit-ML version of the same model, MLR and ML versions with the standardized product declared in MODEL CONSTRAINT, and the original OpenMx model. This separates a difference in standard-error construction from a difference in the fitted numerical solution.

In the closest pair, the Mplus ML constrained product and OpenMx agree to 0.000286 on the standardized estimate, and their delta-method SEs are 0.359 and 0.359. This verifies that the two model parameterizations can represent the same fitted solution. In the selected divergent pair, the Mplus ML constrained estimate is 8.072 whereas OpenMx returns -0.934; changing Mplus from its default MLR to ML does not remove that discrepancy. Thus this part of the gap is optimizer/weak-identification behavior, not a reporting-scale transformation.

For that same stable pair, the current MLR fixed-multiplier SE is 0.405, the MLR product-delta SE is 0.333, and the ML product-delta SE is 0.359. Thus both the post-hoc reporting rule and the MLR-versus-ML choice can move an interval even when the fitted point estimate agrees.

The divergent Mplus outputs nevertheless state that estimation terminated normally. They also report information-matrix condition ratios of about \(1.22\times10^{-14}\) and \(3.61\times10^{-16}\) and explicitly flag possible model nonidentification. The saved current-run rows mark those fits as noncritical, because the VH Mplus-warning screen does not currently treat the CONDITION NUMBER / MODEL NONIDENTIFICATION wording as a critical warning. This is therefore a concrete eligibility-screening gap, rather than evidence that the two models are stably estimating different parameters.

The audit also identifies an inference mismatch in the current VH extraction: its historical-scale Mplus row takes the SE of the raw \(z \leftarrow s\) path and multiplies it by the fitted slope SD. That treats the fitted SD as fixed. Lai’s OpenMx result instead obtains mxSE(stdbeta) for the product itself, including uncertainty in the slope variance and its covariance with the path. The ML MODEL CONSTRAINT audit is the direct Mplus analogue of the latter. This difference can be material, but it is not sufficient to explain every outlying seed because some paired fits have different point estimates before standardization.

At the condition-summary level, the historical OpenMx coverage is also based on a more selective usable-interval population. At \(J=30\), OpenMx retains a mean 91.3% of replications for interval calculation (with some cells near 50%), while current Mplus retains about 98.5%. Therefore the high historical OpenMx coverage should not be read as an engine-only advantage until coverage is recomputed under a common numerical-eligibility rule and a common product-delta estimand.

If params$historical_figure_reference points to a locally saved image of the published Figure 2, render it alongside this panel during review. The visual comparison should ask whether the sign and correlation pattern agree, not whether the current all-method VH analysis matches a method-specific Lai scale.

4. Reporting-scale sensitivity: separate rescaling from estimator behavior

Raw and latent-SD rows report the same fitted estimator on different common condition-level scales. The historical standardized row is different: for the directly comparable methods it preserves Lai’s method-specific multiplier. Consequently, this section is a diagnostic of reporting conventions, not a competition between differently scaled numerical values.

Method-specific historical scaling diagnostics
method_label Mean Lai historical multiplier Availability
Naive dual BLUP 0.407 100.0%
2S-PA 0.493 100.0%
MSEM (VH/Mplus) 0.475 100.0%

The key finding is method-specific: the dual-BLUP distribution shifts downward on Lai’s historical view but is centrally near zero on both common views. Raw-to-latent-SD scaling alone cannot create or remove a bias pattern, because it is a fixed condition-level multiplier applied to both estimate and truth. The extra change on the historical view comes from using the observed EB-slope SD for the naïve method while retaining the true latent-slope SD in the benchmark. This is why a negative historical dual-EB bias can coexist with little central raw-coefficient bias.

5. Slope-SD and reliability diagnostics: test the calibration explanation

The posterior reliability plotted here is calculated from the true full two-dimensional random-effect covariance and Lai’s RMS-scaled within-cluster design. It should not be replaced by lambda22 when random effects are correlated. The first plot removes duplicate values across the number of clusters and \(\beta_{Zu1}\), neither of which enters the posterior-reliability calculation, and shows the remaining determinants explicitly.

True posterior slope reliability varies substantially within every homogeneous cluster-size level
clus_size Minimum reliability Median reliability Maximum reliability
3 0.073 0.465 0.862
10 0.208 0.731 0.953
25 0.397 0.867 0.981

The slope-SD ratios use the same Stage-1 fit attached to the naive dual BLUP raw summary, avoiding duplicate copies of the diagnostics across reporting views. A ratio of one is a diagnostic reference, not a convergence criterion.

The reliability result is consistent with cluster size being an important determinant, but rejects the stronger claim that it is merely a proxy for cluster size: at size 3 the reliability spans approximately .07–.86, and at size 25 it still spans approximately .40–.98. The EB slope SD is most attenuated at low reliability, whereas the fitted slope SD remains close to the population slope SD across the reliability range. This makes the slope-SD correction a useful diagnostic for the observed bias pattern rather than a substitute for modelling reliability itself. Because reliability is emergent rather than independently randomized here, however, a trend against reliability in this study cannot be interpreted as the isolated causal effect of reliability; that is precisely the role of the direct calibration in VH Study 2.

6. Eligibility and convergence: compare the two retention rules directly

VH eligibility and original-Lai eligibility answer different questions. The historical rule retains runs with status_code == 0; the VH-primary rule also applies estimator-specific finite-estimate, finite-SE, design, and fit diagnostics. Next steps and conclusions

The cross-study interpretation here is benchmarked against the current VH Study 2 analysis, with the VH Study 1 analysis used to distinguish the random-effect-as-predictor and random-effect-as-outcome settings.

The overlapping Lai point-estimate result replicates

The strongest conclusion is positive: when method, reporting scale, bias statistic, and eligibility are aligned, the current machinery reproduces Lai’s principal pattern for the estimators that overlap. Dual BLUP is negatively biased on Lai’s historical scale, while 2S-PA and the VH/Mplus MSEM are near zero. The original OpenMx MSEM add-on provides the stricter implementation-and-interval check without changing the VH seven-method bundle. The apparent failure to reproduce a correlation-signed pattern was a terminology mismatch: Lai’s sign-changing lines are slope-only EB models, not the dual-EB model used here.

The remaining replication gap is inferential rather than a broad failure of the DGM or estimator implementation. Dual BLUP intervals are close to Lai’s original aggregate behavior, while 2S-PA is modestly more conservative and VH/Mplus MSEM more anti-conservative in this run. The historical OpenMx MSEM now supplies the original standardized delta-method interval and p-value; a fully strict Figures 3–4 replication still requires all six original methods, especially 2S-PAB and the two slope-only EB specifications.

The scale result narrows what can explain VH Study 2

The historical negative dual-EB bias is not a generic property of using BLUPs as predictors. It is much weaker centrally on the raw and common latent-SD views and becomes prominent when the naïve estimate is multiplied by the shrunken observed EB-slope SD but compared with a truth scaled by the latent slope SD. VH Study 2’s negative raw/common-scale bias in low-reliability conditions therefore cannot be dismissed as the same historical scaling artifact. Its source must lie in estimator behavior, DGM structure, conditioning, or their interaction.

This descriptive bridge resembles the broader VH pattern in one important respect: uncorrected closed-form OLS is negatively biased, particularly when reliability is low, and both Fuller corrections materially reduce that bias. It differs in another: the central naïve dual-BLUP bias in the Lai DGM is near zero or slightly positive across reliability bands, rather than showing the pronounced low-reliability negative raw bias observed in VH Study 2. Rare naïve-BLUP failures remain consequential, so medians, trimmed means, and tail counts should continue to accompany ordinary means.

Reliability is not merely cluster size, but it is not isolated here

The diagnostic range within each homogeneous cluster size is wide enough to reject “reliability is just cluster size” as a description of the Lai DGM. ICC, the slope/intercept variance ratio, and random-effect correlation all matter. Nevertheless, Lai reliability is an emergent combination of these factors rather than a randomized design dimension. Associations in the plot above therefore cannot identify a pure reliability effect. The direct posterior-reliability calibration in the VH project remains essential and is the stronger design for testing reliability-specific hypotheses.

Recommended next analyses

  1. Run a bridge experiment that starts from the Lai DGM and introduces the VH reliability calibration one component at a time. Hold the raw/common reporting scale and eligibility rule fixed, then change the cluster-size design, reliability calibration, and outcome model sequentially. This will localize where the VH low-reliability negative bias enters.
  2. Compare matched reliability bands across Lai and VH using median bias, 20%-trimmed bias, RMSE, and tail-failure counts. Do not rely on the mean alone for naïve BLUP, whose rare failures can dominate it.
  3. Use the source-faithful OpenMx MSEM versus VH/Mplus MSEM contrast to check whether the \(J=30\) coverage gap comes from model parameterization, standardization/SE propagation, or software. Then check 2S-PA interval construction and—if exact paper replication is needed—add 2S-PAB plus the centered and uncentered slope-only EB methods outside the VH bundle.
  4. In VH reporting, keep raw/common latent-SD results primary and retain Lai’s historical method-specific scale only as a labeled diagnostic. Continue to show both eligibility rules and slope-SD ratios so scale, retention, and estimator effects cannot be conflated.

Overall, the replication increases confidence that the shared 2S-PA, VH/Mplus MSEM, and dual-BLUP machinery is recovering Lai’s point-estimate result, while the eighth OpenMx method is designed to provide a source-faithful historical control without changing the VH bundle. It does not explain away the different VH Study 2 pattern. Instead, it sharpens the next question: which aspect of VH’s direct reliability calibration or DGM turns the low-reliability dual-BLUP association negative on a common scale?

Reproducibility notes

The report is parameterized. After generating the Figure 2 post-processing outputs, render it from the repository root with:

quarto render reports/lai_study1_vh_review.qmd \
  -P results_dir:outputs/lai_study1_vh_production_20260731

Optionally supply figure_dir when figures live elsewhere and historical_figure_reference for a locally saved copy of Lai’s published Figure 2. This report does not rerun any models or alter the aggregate output.
